Transcribed by Haadiya Zeeshan
Reviewed by Hibbah Elahi
1
CVP 112
CVP 112
Lungs Anatomy
Olena Bolgova, MD, PhD
Professor of Gross Anatomy
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

2
OBJECTIVES:
OBJECTIVES:
By the end of this lecture students should be able to describe:
◼ Anatomy of right and left bronchi
◼ Anatomy of lungs
◼ Clinical cases:
◼ Aspiration of foreign bodies
◼ Bronchopulmonary segments
◼ Bronchogenic carcinoma (Pancoast tumor)
◼ Pneumonia
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Anatomically, we can subdivide the respiratory system by respiratory tract and 
organs. Respiratory tracts, which provide airflow, can be subdivided into upper and 
lower respiratory tracts.
Upper respiratory tract:
1. Nasal Cavity
2. Pharynx
3. Larynx
Lower respiratory tract:
1. Trachea (after larynx)
2. Bronchi
3
RESPIRATORY SYSTEM
RESPIRATORY SYSTEM
◼ The respiratory system 
includes the lungs and 
respiratory ways that link 
the sites of gas exchange with 
the external environment.
◼ There is also a ventilation 
mechanism, consisting of the 
thoracic cage, intercostal 
muscles, diaphragm, and 
elastic and collagen 
components of the lungs, that 
is important in the movement 
of air through the conducting 
and respiratory parts of the 
lungs.
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

The trachea sits under the cricoid cartilage of the larynx. The thyroid cartilage is 
more prominent in males, but you can palpate it. If you move your finger down and 
feel some thickness, that’s the cricoid cartilage. Once you move your finger even 
lower, right above jugular notch in the sternum, you can feel your trachea. This 
photo is an endoscope (using bronchoscope) of a trachea from inside. The 
bronchoscope has a little camera, light, and some tiny tools we can use to extract 
foreign bodies. Those bumps are C-shaped cartilage. In the trachea, the posterior 
surface has soft tissue for the esophagus, which is needed to swallow food. Once 
the ball of food will swallow through, we need expansion which is done because of 
this soft spot on the back. The trachea is 10 to 13 cm long in adults. It is shorter and 
4
TRACHEA
TRACHEA
◼ It is a thin-walled tube about 
10-13 cm long and 2.5 cm in 
diameter
◼ It consists of 16-20 C-shaped 
rings of hyaline cartilage 
embedded in its fibroelastic wall 
and which serve to keep the 
tracheal lumen patent
◼ It extends from the lower border 
of the cricoid cartilage (C6) in 
the neck to the level of the 
sternal angle (IV disc T4/T5) in 
the superior mediastinum, where 
it divides into the right and left 
primary (main) bronchi
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

narrower in newborns but we still have the same number of cartilages eventually. Once the 
trachea reaches the T4 to T5 intervertebral disc level at the sternal angle (angle of Louis), it 
bifurcates and splits/divides into two main/primary bronchi (bronchi of the first 
generation). At T4, right above of the bifurcation of the trachea, we have the aortic arch. 
The trachea has respiratory epithelium with cilia, which are tiny projections at the top of 
each cell that sweep/propel the mucus upwards. These movements clean the airway 
channels because dust which enters air will settle down in the mucus and needs to be 
constantly removed.
Tracheostomy:
If a patient has blockage of the upper respiratory tracts and cannot breathe, the only 
emergency way we can save their life is by cutting off at the trachea and putting a hook 
shaped tube to provide air to the lungs.
Types of endoscopes:
1. Gastroduodenoscope: stomach
2. Colonoscope: rectum and the large intestine
3. Laparoscope: abdominal cavity
4. Bronchoscope: respiratory ways
4

You cannot see carina in this picture because it's the separation on the inside (needs 
bronchoscope). It is an elevation/ridge (projection) where bifurcation is happening. 
Normally, carina is supposed to stay strictly in the midline, like here.The deviation of 
the carina from the midline is a bad clinical sign indicating that something is pulling 
the carina, most likely a tumour of the lungs (bronchogenic carcinoma). In the 
carina, we have a location with receptors which will initiate a protective cough 
reflex. It is protective because when we cough, we exhale forcefully. With the 
airflow, we eliminate dust and small foreign bodies from our respiratory way. We 
have seven generations of bronchi, after which we have bronchioles split by the 
respiratory duct. C6 means the sixth cervical vertebrae (we have 7).
5
Carina
Carina
◼ It is a ridge separating the 
openings of the main bronchi 
at their junction with the 
trachea
◼ The carina: may be 
examined with a 
bronchoscope and may be 
distorted, widened 
posteriorly, and immobile 
in the presence of 
bronchogenic carcinoma.
◼ The mucous membrane over 
the carina is one of the most 
sensitive areas of the 
tracheobronchial tree and is 
associated with the cough 
reflex
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

Primary/main bronchi (bronchi of first generation):
- The two bronchi after bifurcation 
- They also have the soft spot on the back like the trachea. 
- They are called main/primary because they supply lungs. 
- Once they enter the lungs, they divide into secondary
Secondary/lobar bronchi (bronchi of the second generation):
- 3 on the right and 2 on the left because of the number of lobes in the lungs.

Transcription by: Adam 
Reviewed by: Binish 
Transcription: 
- Last week we covered the nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx and trachea and stopped there. This 
week we continue the conducting portion and cover the respiratory portion of the 
respiratory tract. 
 
1

The lecture covers the structure of each part of the bronchial tree, the difference between 
bronchi and bronchioles, the structure and function of the alveoli, and the structure of the 
pleura. 
Transcription: 
- From the bronchial tree inside the lung, there are two structures you have to know: the 
bronchi and the bronchioles, plus the alveoli. This is the structure of the lung. 
 
2

The respiratory tract is divided functionally into a conducting portion, which cleans and 
humidifies the inspired air and provides conduits for air movement (inside and outside the 
lung), and a respiratory portion, where gas exchange takes place (only inside the lung). 
Transcription: 
- Recap from last lecture: the respiratory system is divided into two parts, the conducting 
portion and the respiratory portion. 
- We consider a part to be respiratory because gas exchange can happen in that area. 
- The last part of the conducting portion is the terminal bronchiole. 
- The first part of the respiratory portion is the one that has alveoli: the respiratory 
bronchiole. 
- This is really very important; you have to know it. 
 
3

The lungs are a pair of spongy, air-filled organs on both sides of the chest, covered by a thin 
layer called the pleura. Each lung is divided into lobes (2 left, 3 right), then bronchopulmonary 
segments (8 left, 10 right), then pulmonary lobules. 
Transcription: 
- We have two lungs, and each is a spongy structure. We have to know the lobes, segments 
and lobules. 
- Left lung: two lobes and eight segments (different books give different numbers; in our 
books it is eight, so we consider eight). 
- Right lung: three lobes and 9 to 10 segments, according to different books. 
- If we divide the segments further, the next level is the lobule. So we have lobes, then 
segments in the middle, then lobules. 
- We will never ask about the number of segments in histology. Stick to the anatomy 
numbers. 
 
4

The trachea divides into the right and left main (primary) bronchi, which enter the hilum of 
each lung. Each primary bronchus divides into lobar (secondary) bronchi: 3 on the right and 2 
on the left, each supplying one lobe. The lobar bronchi give rise to segmental (tertiary) bronchi: 
10 on the right and 8 on the left, each supplying one bronchopulmonary segment. Each 
segment is subdivided into pulmonary lobules, and each lobule is supplied by a bronchiole. 
Transcription: 
- The trachea, with its C-shaped hyaline cartilage, divides into two before it reaches the lung. 
This is the first division, and before it enters the lung we name it the main or primary 
bronchus. 
- Left side: there are two lobes, so the second division gives two branches. We name it the 
lobar bronchus because it supplies the lobe. This is the secondary bronchus. 
- There are eight segments on the left, so the third (tertiary) division gives eight segmental 
bronchi. 
- Right side: one primary bronchus, then three lobar (secondary) bronchi for the three lobes, 
then 9 to 10 segmental (tertiary) bronchi. 
- The segmental bronchi then divide to supply the lobules. These are the bronchioles: the 
bronchiole supplies the lobule. 
- Summary of the divisions: primary (main) → secondary (lobar) → tertiary (segmental) → 
bronchiole. 
- You need to know this by heart, not only in histology. Even in anatomy you need to know 
exactly how we divide the bronchial tree. 
- Histologically, the primary, secondary and tertiary bronchi all have the same histological 
structure. Once we reach the bronchiole, it is a different one. 
5

Initially, the bronchi have the same general structure as the trachea. Where they enter the lungs 
to become intrapulmonary bronchi, the wall changes in two ways: the cartilage rings are 
replaced by irregular cartilage plates around the entire circumference of the wall, and smooth 
muscle is added to form a complete circumferential layer. 
Transcription: 
- Recap of the trachea (four layers, from inside out; this is just memorization): 
o Mucosa: epithelium plus lamina propria. The epithelium is respiratory epithelium. 
o Submucosa: with mucous glands with serous demilunes (mucous cells capped by 
some serous cells). 
o Cartilage: C-shaped hyaline cartilage. 
o Adventitia. 
- When a question comes and the answer is respiratory epithelium, I expect the long name, 
not the word "respiratory": pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, with goblet 
cells if it has goblet cells. If it does not, you do not write them. 
- The trachea has C-shaped cartilage so the esophagus behind it has no problem while we 
swallow. The cartilage is C-shaped and the back is just soft. 
- Inside the lung there is no esophagus to press on, so we do not need the C-shape here. The 
cartilage is a full circle, but not one full plate: it is small pieces (plates) that encircle the 
whole wall. 
 
7

The wall of the intrapulmonary bronchi has five layers. The mucosa is folded because of 
contraction of the smooth muscle in the wall. Its epithelium is ciliated pseudostratified 
epithelium with the same cellular composition as the trachea, and its lamina propria is loose 
connective tissue rich in elastic and collagen fibres with diffuse and nodular lymphatic tissue 
(BALT). 
Transcription: 
- Layers starting from the inside: the mucosa (epithelium plus lamina propria), and the 
epithelium is the same as in the trachea. 
- Why is the mucosa folded? Because there is a smooth muscle layer that was not there 
before. We name this extra layer the muscularis. 
- Then the submucosa (yes, we still have it), the cartilage as small plates making a full circle, 
and the adventitia. 
- So the trachea has four layers and the bronchi have five. 
- Compared with the trachea, the bronchi add three changes: a folded mucosa, a smooth 
muscle layer, and small pieces of cartilage making a full circle. The rest is exactly the same 
as the trachea. 
- Once you see this folding, it means there is muscle. 
 
8

The muscularis is a continuous layer of smooth muscle in large bronchi, more attenuated and 
loosely organized in smaller bronchi, and it regulates the diameter of the airway. The 
submucosa is loose connective tissue with glands in the larger bronchi. The cartilage layer is 
discontinuous hyaline cartilage plates that become smaller as the diameter decreases. The 
adventitia is moderately dense connective tissue continuous with adjacent structures. 
Transcription: 
- Whatever I mentioned here is written in the slides; I did not add anything. 
- Histologically: epithelium (respiratory), lamina propria, smooth muscle, then the small 
pieces of hyaline cartilage, then the adventitia. 
- There is submucosa too, under the muscle: some connective tissue with some very small 
glands. It is not always that clear. 
- There are two things you have to know here: the cartilage and the muscle. The layers are 
otherwise exactly the same. 
- How do I know this section is inside the lung (intrapulmonary)? Because I can see the 
alveoli. Once you see the alveoli, you are inside the lung. 
 
9

Bronchioles are air-conducting ducts that measure 1 mm or less in diameter. Large bronchioles 
branch repeatedly to give the smaller terminal bronchioles, which branch to give the 
respiratory bronchioles. 
Transcription: 
- The bronchiole is less than 1 mm in diameter, so it is very narrow. Some are large and some 
are small. 
- The last part of the conducting portion is the terminal bronchiole. You see how many 
times they ask this: terminal bronchiole, bronchiole, not bronchi. 
- The first part of the respiratory portion is the respiratory bronchiole. 
 
10

The wall of bronchioles is made of a mucosa (epithelium and a lamina propria of loose 
connective tissue with many elastic fibres and no glands), a muscularis (a relatively thick layer 
of smooth muscle in all bronchioles) and an adventitia attached to the surrounding alveoli, with 
occasional lymph nodules or diffuse lymphocytes. Cartilage plates and glands are not present 
in bronchioles. 
Transcription: 
- Bronchioles cannot have many goblet cells. Can we tolerate glands here? No; if we had 
glands it would be a disaster. So there is no submucosa. 
- At this size, do we need cartilage for support? No. So there is no cartilage. 
- So the bronchiole has only three layers: epithelium with lamina propria (mucosa), muscle, 
and adventitia. The muscle layer is thick compared with the bronchi. 
- Two layers are missing compared with the bronchi: no glands (no submucosa) and no 
cartilage. 
- All bronchioles, until the terminal bronchiole, have this structure. 
- Again, we know it is inside the lung because we can see the alveoli. 
 
11

Large bronchioles are initially lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with few 
goblet cells, and smaller bronchioles by simple ciliated columnar or cuboidal epithelium. Goblet 
cells are still present in large bronchioles but not in terminal bronchioles. Club (Clara) cells are 
present in small bronchioles, and their number increases greatly along the length of the 
bronchioles. Occasional brush cells and small granule cells are also present. 
Transcription: 
- The epithelium depends on the size: 
o Large bronchiole: respiratory epithelium, but a little shorter. 
o Smaller: simple columnar. 
o Very narrow: simple cuboidal. We can see this very clearly under the microscope. 
- Goblet cells: as we go inside the lung, we cannot have a lot of mucus, otherwise we would 
be suffocating in our secretions. So there are some goblet cells at the beginning, and they 
become fewer as it gets narrower. 
- Then we have a new cell called the club cell (Clara cell). 
- In the exam, if you are given a bronchiole picture and asked for the lining epithelium, you 
cannot write all of them. Look at the picture, see which type of epithelium it is, and write 
that one. 
 
12

Club (Clara) cells are non-ciliated cells with a rounded or dome-shaped apical surface. They are 
protein-secreting cells. Their functions are to secrete a surface-active agent, a lipoprotein that 
prevents luminal adhesion and airway collapse, particularly during expiration; to produce club 
cell secretory protein (CC16), which has immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory activities; 
and to act as progenitor cells that can differentiate into other epithelial cell types. 
Transcription: 
- Why do we need this cell? It secretes a surfactant-like substance. Surfactant itself is made in 
the alveoli, but we are not yet in the alveoli. At this point the lumen is very narrow, we need 
something to decrease the surface tension, and there are no type II pneumocytes here. This 
is why we have the club cell. 
- Shape: it has no cilia on its surface. This is why we sometimes describe the bronchiolar 
epithelium as having ciliated columnar cells and some non-ciliated cells. 
- It is a protein-forming cell, so the organelles I expect are: rough endoplasmic reticulum 
(protein factory), Golgi, mitochondria for energy, and vesicles (granules) to store what it 
makes. 
- These cells are not easy to find under the light microscope, which is why you will not find 
them in the lab material. 
- It also produces CC16 (club cell protein 16), which has an immunological function: 
anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory for the surrounding environment. 
- Last lecture, respiratory epithelium had five cells: columnar cells, goblet cells, brush cells, 
small granule cells and stem (basal) cells. In simple columnar or cuboidal epithelium there 
are no basal stem cells, so the club cell is the progenitor cell of the epithelial cells in the 
bronchiole. 
13

- These three functions are all important; you have to know them: surfactant-like 
substance, CC16 protein, and progenitor cell. 
- Do not compare it with type I alveolar cells; do not go that way. 
- The name: the cells were described by a scientist named Clara using humans as 
experimental subjects during the Second World War. Very recently the textbooks removed 
his name and now use the word club cell. 
 
14

The presence of cilia beyond the most distal mucus-secreting cells prevents bronchiolar mucus 
accumulation and airflow obstruction. The ciliated cells lining the bronchioles are the beginning 
of the mucociliary escalator. 
Transcription: 
- Can we tolerate goblet cells without cilia in the very small passages of the lung? No. The 
secretions would accumulate in our lung and there would be no way to push them up. 
- This is why the goblet cells have to stop before the cilia stop. This is very important 
structurally. 
- Order of disappearance: the glands stop first, then the goblet cells, then the cilia. So if 
some secretion goes a little further, there are still cilia there to push it up. 
- The function of this area: it is part of the mucociliary escalator. You should know this 
expression. 
 
15

Back to the functional organization: the conducting portion ends at the terminal bronchiole, and 
the respiratory portion, only inside the lung, begins at the respiratory bronchiole. 
Transcription: 
- This is the terminal bronchiole, which has the same three-layer structure. Then all of a 
sudden some alveoli start to appear in the wall of the bronchiole. 
- Once we have alveoli, we stop calling it terminal and call it the respiratory bronchiole. 
 
16

Respiratory bronchioles are a transitional zone involved in both air conduction and gas 
exchange. Their wall has two components: areas lined by simple cuboidal epithelium with 
ciliated cells and club cells (club cells predominate distally) on a lamina propria of elastic fibres 
and smooth muscle, and scattered thin-walled outpocketings, the alveoli, capable of gas 
exchange. 
Transcription: 
- The difference between the terminal and the respiratory bronchiole is the alveoli: they are 
outpocketings from the wall of the bronchiole. 
- The respiratory bronchiole is a transition part: one part is exactly like the terminal 
bronchiole, and the other part has the structure of the alveoli. 
- It is the first part of the respiratory portion because it has alveoli, and in the alveoli gas 
exchange happens. By respiration here I mean gas exchange: taking oxygen and getting rid 
of carbon dioxide. 
- Identifying the respiratory bronchiole is one of the very common questions in the OSPE. 
The terminal bronchiole has no outpocketings; I know this one is respiratory because I can 
see the alveoli in its wall. 
- Layers of the bronchiolar part: the lining is simple cuboidal, with only a single layer of round 
nuclei. No options here, because there is no space for simple columnar. 
- There are a lot of club cells and no goblet cells (we cannot have them). Then the smooth 
muscle (muscularis) layer, then the adventitia. 
 
17

Alveolar ducts are elongated airways with almost no walls, only alveoli, as their peripheral 
boundary; rings of smooth muscle are present in the knob-like interalveolar septa. Alveolar sacs 
are spaces surrounded by clusters of alveoli that open into them. They usually occur at the end 
of an alveolar duct but may occur anywhere along its length. 
Transcription: 
- There are two structures you have to know here: a long one and a rounded one. 
- The long one is a pathway with no wall, made only by the openings of the alveoli: the 
alveolar duct. 
- The rounded one is like a bunch of grapes, a distended space made by alveoli: the alveolar 
sac. 
- Very simple: if it is long, it is a duct; if it is distended, it is a sac. 
- Do ducts or sacs have club cells? No. The last part with club cells is the respiratory 
bronchiole. Once we have only alveoli, there are no club cells and no respiratory epithelium; 
there are different cells, covered next. 
 
18

Alveoli are the terminal air spaces of the respiratory system and the actual site of gas exchange 
between air and blood. Each adult lung has about 150 to 250 million alveoli. Each is a 
thin-walled polyhedral chamber about 0.2 mm in diameter, surrounded by a network of 
capillaries that brings blood close to the inhaled air. 
Transcription: 
- There are millions of alveoli, about 150 to 250 million, a very big number. 
- Each is a very small structure (about 0.2 mm in diameter, as on the slide). 
- The cells of the alveolus: 
o Two cells make the wall: type I and type II pneumocytes (alveolar cells). 
o There are also macrophages, but they wander inside the lumen. They are not 
attached and do not make the wall. 
 
19

Type I alveolar cells (type I pneumocytes) are extremely thin squamous cells. They make up 
only 40% of the alveolar-lining cells but line 95% of the alveolar surface. They are joined to one 
another and to the other alveolar cells by occluding junctions and are not capable of cell 
division. Function: gas exchange, forming part of the air-blood barrier. 
Transcription: 
- Type I cells are very flat, long cells. This is why they are only 40% of the cells lining the 
alveoli but cover 95% of the surface area. 
- Function: gas exchange, and they form the blood-air barrier. These are the two important 
functions you have to know. 
- Can they regenerate? No. 
- Can we allow fluid to pass between the cells? No. This is why they are attached to each 
other by tight (occluding) junctions. 
- Remember: 40% of the cells, covering 95%, occluding junctions, gas exchange and part of 
the blood-air barrier, and they cannot regenerate. It is that simple; do not complicate it. 
 
20

Type II alveolar cells (type II pneumocytes or septal cells) are secretory, cuboidal cells 
interspersed among type I cells that tend to congregate at septal junctions. They make up 60% 
of the alveolar-lining cells but cover only about 5% of the surface, and they bulge into the 
alveolar space. Their apical cytoplasm is filled with lamellar bodies. Functions: progenitor cells 
for type I and type II cells, and secretion of surfactant. 
Transcription: 
- If type I is 40%, type II is 60%. If type I covers 95%, and there are only these two cells, type II 
covers only 5%. 
- The other cell cannot regenerate, so type II is the stem cell for both type I and type II. 
- Compare: the stem cell in the bronchiole is the club cell; the stem cell of the alveolus is the 
type II cell. 
- Type II is the one that projects into the lumen. Type I is squamous; type II is cuboidal. 
- Other names: secretory cell, because it secretes surfactant, and septal cell, because it is 
usually found close to the septum. 
- Function: production of surfactant, which decreases the surface tension so the alveoli do 
not collapse. 
 
21

Surfactant is a surface-active agent synthesized by type II pneumocytes and stored in lamellar 
bodies. It is an oily mixture of phospholipids (the most critical is DPPC), neutral lipids and 
surfactant proteins. DPPC accounts for almost all of its surface-tension-reducing properties. 
Functions: it decreases alveolar surface tension and actively participates in the clearance of 
foreign materials. 
Transcription: 
- Something very unique to the type II cell: the vesicle that stores surfactant. The surfactant is 
arranged as layers inside the vesicle, which is why we call it the lamellar body. 
- It is a very unique structure that you cannot find in any other place. Once you see a lamellar 
body, this is a type II cell. 
- Surfactant has three parts: phospholipids, neutral lipids and proteins. The structure is not 
that important in histology. 
- The most important component is the phospholipid (DPPC), which is responsible for 
decreasing the surface tension. I want this information. 
- Functions: decreasing the surface tension, plus some immunological function, like cleaning 
the surface. 
 
22

Surfactant is secreted by exocytosis to form a thin layer lining the alveoli. Without enough 
surfactant, the alveoli would collapse with each exhalation. This happens in preterm infants 
whose lungs cannot yet produce enough surfactant, leading to neonatal respiratory distress 
syndrome (RDS). 
Transcription: 
- Surfactant comes out by exocytosis, a highly active transport. Once it is out, it covers the 
whole surface of the alveoli to decrease the surface tension. 
- A baby delivered in the seventh month: the lung is not developed, so we keep him in the 
incubator until the cells that produce surfactant become well developed. 
- The disease is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, in babies with immature lungs, 
mostly preterm babies. 
- From the questions: once they start breathing normally, they no longer have RDS. They are 
given medication to enhance this process, so they do not stay in the incubator for long. 
 
23

Alveolar macrophages are derived from blood monocytes and belong to the mononuclear 
phagocyte system. Alveolar macrophages function in the air space of the alveolus and remove 
inhaled particles such as dust and pollen (dust cells) and red blood cells that may enter the 
alveoli in heart failure (heart failure cells). Engorged macrophages pass up the bronchial tree in 
the mucus and are disposed of by swallowing or expectoration. 
Transcription: 
- The mother cell of the macrophage is the monocyte, the same family as the microglia you 
remember. 
- One type lives inside the alveolus: the alveolar macrophage. It works like a vacuum, 
scavenging anything we do not want from the surface. If dust reaches this part, the cell eats 
the dust, which is why we call it the dust cell. 
- In heart failure, patients get pulmonary hypertension. The pressure pushes some red blood 
cells into the alveoli, where they should not be. The macrophages eat them and become 
darker. These are called heart failure cells. 
- After some time the cell is filled with particles and we have to get rid of it. How does it reach 
the parts with cilia? These cells have no cilia, but they have pseudopodia, so they can move 
until they reach the closest part that has cilia. The cilia then push them up to the pharynx. 
- There they are either swallowed (mostly), and the HCl helps, or, if the cough is strong 
enough, they are coughed out. 
 
24

Septal macrophages reside in the connective tissue of the interalveolar septa. They are filled 
with accumulated phagocytosed material and may remain in the septa for much of a person's 
life. Both alveolar and septal macrophages increase in smokers. 
Transcription: 
- The other option: if the cell cannot be taken out, it squeezes between the cells and goes to 
live in the septum. This is why we call it the septal macrophage. 
- It is a cell that has already done its function inside. We do not want it anymore, so we just 
keep it here, for life. 
- This is a problem in smokers, because the number of these cells increases a lot, and over 
time I think it affects the function of the lung. 
- So there are two macrophages, or the same cell in a different situation: the alveolar 
macrophage (scavenger, also called dust cell or heart failure cell) and the septal 
macrophage (stays for life, increased in smokers). In the picture you can see the difference 
in color. 
- From the questions: the alveolar macrophage can pass between the cells to reach the 
septum. 
 
25

The interalveolar septum is thin connective tissue between adjacent alveolar air spaces. Its wall 
is a network of elastic and reticular fibres; the elastic fibres are responsible for the stretching 
and recoil of the alveoli during respiration. It has a rich capillary network from the pulmonary 
artery and is the site of the air-blood barrier. Alveolar pores (of Kohn) penetrate the septa and 
connect neighbouring alveoli that open into different bronchioles, allowing air to circulate from 
one alveolus to another. 
Transcription: 
- If I want to say one structure inside the interalveolar septum, it is the elastic fibres. The 
main function of the alveoli is to stretch and recoil, so we cannot ignore them. 
- Imagine a bronchus, a bronchiole and its alveoli. If I put a block in one bronchiole, nothing 
reaches its alveoli, and they would collapse. 
- But between the alveoli there are openings called the pores of Kohn. If only one bronchiole 
is blocked, its alveoli are still ventilated through these pores from the neighbouring alveoli. 
The air concentration will be higher in one than the other, but it is still functioning. 
- Without these pores, whatever block happened, the whole part would collapse. 
- This is normal, not pathological. 
- The most important structure that you cannot forget in the septum is the elastic fibres. 
And the pores connecting the alveoli are the pores of Kohn. 
 
26

The air-blood barrier (respiratory membrane) is the cells and cell products across which gases 
diffuse between the alveolar and capillary compartments. Its thin portion is made of a thin 
layer of surfactant, a type I epithelial cell and its basal lamina, and a capillary endothelial cell 
and its basal lamina. These two basal laminae are often fused. Most gas exchange occurs in the 
thin portion. 
Transcription: 
- Layers of the blood-air barrier, in order, from the air to the blood: 
o Surfactant (the liquid lining). 
o Type I pneumocyte. 
o Fused basement membranes (of the type I cell and the endothelium). 
o Endothelium of the capillary. 
- It has to be in order. This part is also called the respiratory membrane. 
- There is a thin portion and a thick portion. The thin portion is very important, and its 
function is gas exchange. 
 
27

The thick portion contains connective tissue cells (such as macrophages and fibroblasts) and 
fibres between the two basal laminae. It is thought to be where tissue fluid accumulates before 
being drained into the lymphatic vessels. 
Transcription: 
- In the thick portion there is a space between the two alveoli. Why do we need it? 
- We cannot tolerate any fluid inside the alveoli, so any extra fluid has to go somewhere. It 
goes here. 
- This space has a few connective tissue cells, like macrophages and fibroblasts. 
- Function: it accumulates any extra fluid in the lung for a very short time, until it reaches the 
lymphatic vessels. 
 
28

The pleura is a serous membrane that covers the outer surface of the lung and the internal wall 
of the thoracic cavity. The parietal pleura lines the internal thoracic walls, and the visceral 
pleura tightly covers the outer surface of each lung. The two layers are continuous at the hilum 
of each lung. 
Transcription: 
- You already had the pericardium. The pleura is exactly the same; nothing changes. 
- The layer touching the lung is the visceral pleura, the one lining the thoracic wall from 
inside is the parietal pleura, and between them is the pleural cavity. 
 
29

Both pleurae are made of simple squamous mesothelial cells on a thin connective tissue layer 
with collagen and elastic fibres, which allows flexibility during breathing. The pleural cavity is a 
narrow space between the parietal and visceral layers, lined by mesothelium. Mesothelial cells 
produce a thin film of serous fluid that acts as a lubricant, so the surfaces slide smoothly during 
respiratory movement. 
Transcription: 
- The lining is mesothelium (simple squamous epithelium). 
- Its function is producing serous fluid, exactly the same as in the pericardium. 
- Is there a lamina propria under it? Yes. If there were no connective tissue under the 
epithelium, how would these cells survive? We have to have connective tissue under the 
epithelium. 
 
30

Bronchial asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways (genetic and environmental 
factors), with wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath and chest tightness. The bronchiolar 
epithelium has more goblet cells and a thick basement membrane, with a thick hyperplastic 
smooth muscle layer. 
Transcription: 
- There are a few disease names you have to know. You will mostly see them in the TBL and 
in the final exam, in the cases. I do not want the pathology at all, but when you see 
bronchial asthma, understand that I am talking mostly about the bronchioles, and with 
emphysema I am talking about the alveoli. 
- These patients, mostly kids seen in the pediatric clinic, come with wheezing and cannot take 
their breath. 
- The cause is sometimes genetic and sometimes environmental, most commonly dust in the 
air. 
- Why is the drawing a bronchiole and not a bronchus? There is no cartilage. It has three 
layers: epithelium, muscle and adventitia. 
- What happens: a lot of thick secretion, so many goblet cells, and a thick muscle layer. It is a 
problem in the bronchioles. 
 
31

Emphysema is a chronic lung disease most commonly caused by cigarette smoking. It involves 
dilatation and permanent enlargement of the air spaces with destruction of the alveolar wall. 
The main symptom is shortness of breath, which usually begins gradually. 
Transcription: 
- Emphysema is common in those who smoke. 
- The interalveolar septa are destroyed. Imagine several alveoli; at the end there is only one 
space because many septa have disappeared. 
- So there is less surface area for gas exchange, and they complain of shortness of breath. 
 
32

Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder with production of thick, viscous mucus from almost all 
exocrine glands. The mucociliary escalator malfunctions, so the thick mucus accumulates, and 
patients have frequent respiratory infections. 
Transcription: 
- It is genetic and affects multiple organs, but it affects the lung too. 
- In the lung there is very thick mucus. This is very important: the cilia are functioning, but 
they cannot push the thick mucus. So the patients drown in their secretions. 
- You should at least know these three, and also the clinical items from last time, because 
they are mostly in the TBL and the final. 
33

P17. Lung Volumes 
    red = the doctor said it is important  |  green = meh, not needed or just for understanding 
 
SLIDE 18: LUNG VOLUMES 
 
• After a maximal exhalation we still cannot get the lung empty. 1.5 L remains in the lung and that 
volume is called the residual volume 
• Lung volume = how much gas we have in the lung. It depends on the phase of breathing: the 
volume after maximal exhalation is different from after normal exhalation, after a tidal breath and 
after maximal inspiration 
• The lung volume changes between 1.5 L and 6 L 
• We define these volumes to bring some structure into it, and to be able to measure them when they 
change, for example in disease 
• We learned yesterday that when lung volume increases or decreases, it is the volume of the 
respiratory zone (alveolar region) that changes. The dead space volume is very small (about 150 
mL) and stays constant 
• Residual volume (RV) = the volume at the end of a maximal exhalation. It cannot be expired any 
more 
• After a normal exhalation the volume is larger than that. The difference between normal and 
maximal exhalation is the expiratory reserve volume (ERV). Reserve because if we need to, we can 
exhale it 
• At the end of a normal exhalation we inhale normally. Yesterday's example was 450 mL but 
normally it is half a litre. This is the tidal volume (VT) 
• We can still inhale much more with maximal inspiratory force. The difference between a maximal 
and a normal inspiration is 2.5 L, the inspiratory reserve volume (IRV). Reserve because normally 
we breathe in to here, but if we need more air we can inhale more 
• So there are 4 lung volumes: RV, ERV, VT, IRV

• ERV, VT and IRV can be mobilised by breathing (I can exhale and inhale them). RV cannot, 
because we cannot exhale it 
• Can we measure them? The 3 we can mobilise are simple to measure: exhale into a bag and 
measure how much. RV cannot be done that way, it needs a separate method 
• We measure the 3 first. A simple classic method is the spirometer

SLIDE 19: SPIROMETER 
 
• A spirometer is just a chamber containing air (yellow, top) with water at the bottom. The water has 
no function except letting the top of the device move in and out without producing pressure (things 
float in water) 
• We fill it with air and connect the person, with the nose closed so he cannot breathe to the outside. 
His lung is directly connected to the spirometer gas, so the lung and the spirometer make a closed 
system. Nothing comes in or goes out 
• When he inhales, lung volume increases and spirometer volume decreases. The increase in lung 
volume equals the decrease in spirometer volume, so we can measure the lung volume change 
indirectly from the spirometer 
• The spirometer is connected by a rope to a pen writing on paper. Inhale: the top of the spirometer 
moves down, the rope is pulled up, the pen goes up, so inspiration is written upwards. Exhale: air 
moves into the spirometer, the top goes up, the rope comes down, the pen writes downwards 
• Normal breathing: in and out between the end of normal inspiration and the end of normal expiration 
= tidal volume 
• Ask him to exhale maximally: the difference between maximal and normal exhalation = ERV. Ask 
him to inhale maximally: the difference between maximal and normal inspiration = IRV 
• We have measured VT, ERV and IRV. We could not measure RV, because it cannot be exhaled, so 
that volume is missing

SLIDE 20: MEASURING RESIDUAL VOLUME (HELIUM DILUTION) 
 
• Now we want to measure the missing volume, the residual volume 
• Analogy: 2 glasses of water, one drop of blue ink in each. The bigger glass is paler. From the 
intensity of the colour you can work out the volume: if one glass has double the volume, its 
concentration is half. That is the dilution method 
• In the lung we use a gas that is not used and not produced in the body. If the volume is large the 
gas is diluted more, if small, less. This is the helium dilution method 
• Same spirometer but with a valve. We close it so the person cannot breathe in and out of the 
spirometer. The nose is closed in the figure but while setting up the nose must be open, otherwise 
he cannot breathe and will die. Imagine the picture without the nose clip 
• Fill the spirometer with a certain volume of air, e.g. 5 L (Vs), and inject a little helium. It spreads 
through the spirometer volume. The valve is closed so it cannot enter the lung 
• Take a sample and measure the helium concentration. For gas mixtures we use the fraction (O2 
was 0.21). F0 = 0.1, so 10% helium and 90% air 
• We want the amount of helium. Concentration = amount / volume, so amount = concentration × 
volume. Remember this, we need it all the time in physiology 
• The volume that contains helium is only the spirometer volume (no helium in the lung yet). Amount 
before mixing = F0 × Vs 
• Now close the nose and open the valve. He breathes from the spirometer and the helium spreads 
over the lung volume too, so the concentration falls. F1 = 0.08: from 10% to 8% 
• Amount after mixing = F1 × (Vs + VL). The volume is now spirometer plus lung 
• Did the amount of helium change? No. The concentration and the volume changed but the amount 
stays the same, because the helium is not used or produced in the body. 1 g before, 1 g after 
• So put an equal sign: F0 × Vs = F1 × (Vs + VL). F0, Vs and F1 are known, only VL is unknown, so 
we can solve for it

WHICH LUNG VOLUME IS VL? 
• It depends on when you open the valve. VL is whatever is in the lung at that moment 
• At the end of a maximal exhalation = RV 
• At the end of a normal exhalation = RV + ERV = FRC 
• At the end of a normal inhalation = RV + ERV + VT 
• At the end of a maximal inhalation = TLC (all of them together) 
• To measure RV: open the nose, tell him to exhale maximally, then close the nose and open the 
valve 
THE MISTAKE 
• If he does not exhale maximally, the lung volume is larger than RV and you think it is RV. It is an 
easy mistake to make 
• His example: he did not exhale fully, you measure 3 L instead of 1.5 L, think "huge RV, probably 
emphysema" and give medication. A month later you repeat it correctly, get 1.5 L and say "one 
month of therapy and you went from emphysema to healthy". But emphysema is not reversible, so 
the first measurement was just wrong 
• Point: it is a simple procedure but mistakes have real consequences for the patient. As a physician 
you have a lot of accountability, so be serious about these measurements 
• Student question: how do you know the lung volume if you start with 5 L? Answer: the 5 L is only 
the spirometer. When the valve opens, the only thing added is the lung volume, nothing else

SLIDE 21: LUNG CAPACITIES 
 
 
• We have 4 volumes and also 4 capacities. Capacity = sum of 2 or more lung volumes. If you hear 
capacity, think at least 2 volumes 
• RV + ERV = functional residual capacity (FRC), about 3 L. The volume in the lung at the end of a 
normal exhalation 
• VT + IRV = inspiratory capacity (IC): 0.5 + 2.5 = 3 L 
• ERV + VT + IRV = vital capacity (VC). The maximal volume you can mobilise 
• All 4 volumes together = total lung capacity (TLC) 
• VC is the maximum possible tidal volume: breathe out maximally and then in maximally. ERV and 
IRV are reserves for the tidal volume, so VT can grow at their cost until both become zero and VT = 
VC. That is why they are called reserve volumes 
 
IS THE VOLUME WE CANNOT EXHALE A GOOD THING? 
• Yes, it is positive. Reasons: 
– Surface tension: if the lung collapsed it would be very hard to reinflate, like blowing up a 
balloon that is completely empty (hard at the start, easier after a bit of air). It would need much 
more muscle force, which is a waste of energy. It is more economical not to empty the lung 
– Speech and thinking would be interrupted every time the lung was empty 
– Gas exchange stays continuous. If the lung were empty there would be no exchange of O2 and 
CO2 between gas and blood at that moment. The gas that stays guarantees continuous 
exchange 
– Alveolar gas stays stable. The FRC (3 L) is "used" air with 14% O2 and 7% CO2, while fresh 
gas has 21% O2 and 0% CO2. If we emptied the lung each time, the concentrations would 
swing dramatically and these changes would also show in the blood. The receptors that 
measure PO2 and PCO2 and adjust breathing would "go crazy"

SLIDE 22: EFFECTS OF AGEING ON LUNG VOLUMES 
 
• These volumes depend on many things: gender, size, physical training and so on. So compare the 
measured volumes with the average of a group of people 
• Ageing: after birth the lung volume (TLC) is very small. It increases sharply up to age 20, then only 
a little. RV also increases after 20, slowly, but RV increases sharply after 60 (he is 75, so for him it 
goes sharply up) 
• RV is the volume I cannot mobilise. The volume I can mobilise is the difference between TLC and 
RV, which is the vital capacity 
• As we age, the volume we can use for breathing (VC) gets smaller and the volume that does not 
help (RV) gets bigger 
• This is a typical sign of emphysema: RV increases, TLC stays about the same and VC decreases. 
So elderly people are functionally like a person with a little emphysema

SLIDE 23: IDEAL GAS LAW 
 
• The volume of a gas depends on temperature and pressure: high pressure and low temperature 
make it shrink, low pressure and high temperature make it expand 
• We measure lung volumes indirectly from the gas that comes out. We are really interested in how 
big the "room" in the lung is, not the air, but we cannot go into the lung and measure it, so we use 
the gas volume 
• The spirometer is at room temperature (about 20 °C) and the body is 37 °C, so the gas volume in 
the spirometer is smaller than the real lung volume. We must correct volumes to the body 
conditions 
• By the ideal gas law there are 3 conditions: BTPS (body: temperature, pressure, saturated with 
water vapour), ATPS (ambient, the spirometer) and STPD (standard). We measure under ATPS 
and convert to BTPS. Converting ATPS to BTPS increases the volume by about 10%

SLIDE 24: CONVERSION OF VOLUMES 
 
• Conversion factors come from the ideal gas law. I could do it all for you but it is not necessary 
• He said you can forget these, do not memorise them or learn them from the slides (not tested) 
• Why: devices today either measure at the correct body temperature or have software that makes 
the correction, so they give you the BTPS volume directly. It matters only if you are sent to a rural 
area with no modern device and a normal spirometer. Then you must remember that the measured 
volume is not the volume in the lung and convert it to BTPS. When he became a physician every 
volume had to be converted with these equations, now the device does it

SLIDE 25: CAUSES OF REDUCED VITAL CAPACITY 
 
• There are a lot of diseases that reduce the vital capacity (the volume you can mobilise): skeletal 
abnormality, weak respiratory muscles, lung diseases and airway obstruction 
• Point: measuring lung volumes is important because they are affected by diseases of the airways, 
lung, muscle and skeleton 
• Do not memorise these diseases and you will not be asked about them. You learn them in 
pathology later. They are just examples

SLIDE 26: CHANGES IN LUNG VOLUMES IN RESPIRATORY DISEASES 
 
• This is what you have to know and never forget: from a functional point of view respiratory diseases 
are divided into 2 categories, obstructive and restrictive 
• Obstructive (e.g. emphysema): as said before, RV increases very much. Because RV is part of 
TLC, TLC increases a little. So the ratio RV / TLC is high. You could see the same on the ageing 
curve above 60 
• Restrictive: all lung volumes decrease, but proportionately. If one volume decreases by 20%, the 
other decreases by 20% too, so RV / TLC stays normal 
• From this ratio alone you can differentiate an obstructive from a restrictive disease
